chunks: Ali ibn Mahziyar from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Hammad from Hariz from Zurarah who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far and his son (peace be upon them): A man has abundant produce from various kinds, or wealth in which no single category reaches the threshold for zakat. Is he obligated to pay one zakat on all of it? They said: 'No. It becomes obligatory only when it is complete, so zakat is obligatory on each category individually. If his land produces various kinds of produce, each amount being below the threshold for zakat, then one zakat is not obligatory on them collectively.'

Zurarah said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man has one hundred and ninety dirhams and thirty-nine dinars. Should he pay zakat on it? He said: 'No, there is no zakat upon him regarding the dirhams nor the dinars until he completes forty dinars and two hundred dirhams.'
Zurarah said: And so it is with all things.

And I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man had four camels, thirty-nine sheep, and twenty-nine cows. Should he pay zakat on them? He said: 'He does not pay zakat on any of them because none of them is complete, so zakat is not obligatory on them.'
ai.seo_question: How is zakat calculated when a person has multiple types of wealth, each below the minimum threshold?
ai.summary: This narration from the Ahl al-Bayt clarifies the Shia jurisprudential principle of 'separate nisab' (istifrad), where different asset classes like gold, silver, and livestock are evaluated independently rather than aggregated. It highlights the practical application of this rule by detailing specific thresholds for dinars, dirhams, and animals, ensuring that minor deficiencies in one category do not trigger zakat liability for the entire wealth. This distinction is crucial in Shia fiqh for distinguishing between mixed wealth and distinct categories, reflecting the precise legal methodology of the Imams.
